newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Revamped S.Africa farm bill seen adopted Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: Revamped S.Africa farm bill seen adopted Wednesday.

text.p: South Africa's Parliament will debate a far-reaching proposal on Wednesday to abolish statutory agricultural market controls and point the country towards a freer and more accessible industry.

Former Agriculture Minister Kraai van Niekerk's original Marketing of Agricultural Products Bill, which sought largely to bolster the status quo, was completely rewritten by parliament's select committee on agriculture and land affairs.
The measure, which has been approved by the Senate, enters the National Assembly with its passage assured by the dominance of the ruling African National Congress.

"It's going to free up processes for people to compete on an equal footing...to be far more responsive to consumers and far more adept at allowing efficient and effective farmers to prevail," select committee chair Janet Love said in an interview.

The revised bill will help agriculture boost its contribution to GDP and to economic growth, she said. It proposes a 10-member National Agricultural Marketing Council (NAMC) with a small full-time secretariat to advise the minister of agriculture.
"Although there is a movement towards a freer market, the necessity for intervention is accepted under certain circumstances," Love said.

At the request of any of five "directly affected" groups -- producers, including labour, vendors, buyers, processors and consumers -- the NAMC can advise the minister to intervene in a specific market or region for of up to two years.
Intervention can take the form of a levy of up to five percent of the producer's profit, an export control mechanism, pools, obligatory record keeping or a register of producers.
Any measure approved would have to meet one of the following four aims without undermining any of the others:
- Increasing market access for all market participants;
- Improved efficiency of agricultural marketing;
- Optimisation of agricultural export earnings;
- Enhanced viability of the agricultural sector.
The bill also prohibits any measure that would undermine national food security, fair labour practice or the overall number of jobs in the economy.
"This bill is designed to ensure that if there are interventions, those interventions will be exceptional and designed to fulfill very specific objectives over a limited time," Love said.
She said one of the committee's primary objectives in drafting the bill had been to open agricultural markets to a much broader range of farmers.
"If you look at the agricultural sector today, it is overwhelmingly commercial and overwhelmingly white," she said.
The bill would break the commercial stranglehold without undermining food security and without pushing up prices. Single channel marketing will end with the implementation of the bill.
"The government is for the first time obliged to take seriously some level of obligation to actively increase the access within a market," Love said.
With the removal of apartheid-era controls, agriculture would have to become more responsive to international trends and market conditions.
"I see the market becoming more vibrant and I see the market gaining new entrants. I have absolutely no doubt that our overall agricultural production is going to increase."
"Prices will change. They will be much more influenced by the international market than they are today. In some cases, I'm sure they will become more volatile.
"We will have to be more responsive to international prices. People will obviously resist not being able to import commodities offered at a price significantly lower than here."
Van Niekerk was replaced by former Land Affairs Minister Derek Hanekom when F.W. de Klerk's National Party quit the government of national unity at the end of June.
